name: Ramesses II
info: Ramesses II, known as Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty; he reigned for 66 years from 1279 BCE and is remembered for the Battle of Kadesh, a peace treaty with the Hittites and his monuments.

facts.born: c. 1303 BCE, into a family from the far north-eastern nome of Egypt; son of Seti I and grandson of Ramesses I, a vizier and military officer who became pharaoh
facts.died: 1213 BCE (13 August by the most detailed reckoning; others give July or early August), aged about 90, most likely at Pi-Ramesses; cause unknown, possibly an infection from an abscess in the jaw
facts.role: Prince regent under his father Seti I from about the age of fourteen; third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt, 1279–1213 BCE
facts.known: The Battle of Kadesh against the Hittites; the Treaty of Kadesh; the temples of Abu Simbel; the Ramesseum at Thebes; the Delta capital Pi-Ramesses; a 66-year reign with thirteen or fourteen Sed festivals; the Greek name Ozymandias

t: Ramesses II ruled Egypt for 66 years, the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh, and built from the Delta to Nubia on a scale no earlier king had matched.
He claimed Kadesh as a great victory, but the battle is generally considered a stalemate, and the war with the Hittites ended in Year 21 in a treaty of which both versions survive.
His monuments served as propaganda for his victories and his divinity, and he was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a god in his own lifetime.
dyk: In September 1976 the mummy of Ramesses II was sent to France for treatment and received at Paris–Le Bourget Airport with full military honours befitting a king. The persistent claim that it was issued with a passport for the journey is incorrect.
ev: Ramesses is born, the grandson of the vizier and officer who became pharaoh as Ramesses I
He succeeds his father Seti I as pharaoh at the age of 25
He fights the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II at Kadesh in Syria, a battle generally considered a stalemate
Returning to Syria, his armies take Moab and recapture Upi, the land around Damascus
He concludes the peace known as the Treaty of Kadesh with the Hittite king Ḫattušili III
With his queen Nefertari he travels into Nubia to inaugurate the temple of Abu Simbel
He dies aged about 90, early in his 67th regnal year, and is succeeded by his son Merneptah

sections.early:
Ramesses II was not born a prince. His grandfather, Ramesses I, was a vizier and military officer under the pharaoh Horemheb, who appointed him as his successor; Ramesses II was then about eleven years old. When Ramesses I died, his son Seti I became king, and at about the age of fourteen Ramesses II was designated prince regent. The family came from the far north-eastern nome of Egypt rather than from the south, as the Twelfth, Seventeenth and Eighteenth Dynasties had, a point the Egyptologist Frank J. Yurco drew from the features of the king's mummy. It also had ties to the god Set: Seti's name means "follower of Set", and Ramesses I had served as High Priest of Set under Amenhotep III.

The Egypt he grew up in was that of the New Kingdom, the most powerful period of ancient Egypt. Nubia, south of the first cataract of the Nile, had been a colony for 200 years, but territories once held had been lost to the Nubians and the Hittites. Seti I had made a triumphal entry into the Syrian city of Kadesh about a decade before his son fought there, and he kept a summer palace in the eastern Delta on the site his son later made a capital. Ramesses may have been present on his father's Libyan campaigns, to which records such as the Aswan Stele of his second year perhaps hark back. When he was about 22, two of his own sons, including Amun-her-khepeshef, accompanied him on at least one campaign in Nubia; reliefs at Beit el-Wali show him charging tribes south of Egypt in a war chariot, with his young sons behind him in chariots of their own.
sections.rise:
Ramesses came to the throne on a day recorded as III Shemu, day 27, which most Egyptologists take to be 31 May 1279 BCE; he was 25. In the early part of the reign he gave his attention to building cities, temples and monuments, and in his third year he began what has been called the most ambitious building project since the pyramids, raised almost 1,500 years earlier. He also set out to recover lost territories and to secure Egypt's borders. The Egyptian army of his reign is estimated at some 100,000 men.

In his second year he defeated the Sherden sea pirates, who had been attacking cargo vessels on the sea routes to Egypt. He posted troops and ships along the coast, let the pirates attack what they took for prey, and captured them in a single action, probably near the mouth of the Nile; the Lukka and the Shekelesh were defeated in the same battle. Many Sherden, with horned helmets and round shields, appear soon afterwards in the pharaoh's bodyguard.

In the fourth year he campaigned in Syria, set up the first of the stelae at Nahr el-Kalb near what is now Beirut, and captured Amurru, a vassal state of the Hittites. He founded a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the eastern Delta, possibly to be closer to his territories in Canaan and Syria, though his motives are uncertain. Its workshops are supposed to have produced some 1,000 weapons in a week, about 250 chariots in two weeks and 1,000 shields in a week and a half. From there he moved against the Hittite Empire, a more substantial enemy than any he had yet faced.
sections.deeds:
The Battle of Kadesh, in his fifth year, was fought against the Hittite forces of Muwatalli II. After a month's advance through Canaan, according to the Egyptian sources, Ramesses reached Kadesh on 1 May 1274 BCE. His troops were caught in an ambush: Hittite chariotry broke through his second division and attacked his camp. Reinforced by other divisions, the Egyptians counterattacked and routed the Hittites, whose survivors swam the Orontes to the city walls. Unable to sustain a long siege, Ramesses returned to Egypt.

Late in his seventh year he went back to Syria. One force, under his son Amun-her-khepeshef, took Edom-Seir and Moab; the other, under the king, attacked Jerusalem and Jericho, and the reunited army recaptured Upi, the land around Damascus. In his eighth and ninth years he pushed north into Amurru and besieged and took Dapur, where no Egyptian soldier had been seen since Thutmose III, almost 120 years earlier. In Year 21 (1259 BCE) he concluded with the Hittite king Ḫattušili III the peace known as the Treaty of Kadesh, whose 18 articles survive in an Egyptian and a Hittite version. No Egyptian campaigns in Canaan are mentioned after it.

He built from the Delta to Nubia, "covering the land with buildings in a way no monarch before him had". Besides Pi-Ramesses, his largest works were the Ramesseum, a mortuary temple in western Thebes with an enthroned statue of the king 17 metres high and weighing more than 1,000 tonnes, and the temple complex of Abu Simbel in Nubia, which he and his queen Nefertari travelled to inaugurate in 1255 BCE.
sections.opponents:
His chief opponents were the Hittites. Ramesses claimed a great victory at Kadesh, and he held the battlefield, but the battle is generally considered a stalemate and the Hittites the ultimate victors of the campaign: the Egyptians retreated, and Hittite forces invaded and briefly occupied the Egyptian possessions around Damascus. Egypt's sphere was reduced to Canaan, where princes, seemingly goaded on by the Hittites, began revolts. The northern conquests that followed proved ephemeral. The strip between Amurru and Kadesh returned to the Hittite fold within a year, so that he had to march on Dapur again in his tenth year, and that second success was as meaningless as the first, since neither power could decisively defeat the other.

The peace itself grew out of a crisis. Ḫattušili III had deposed his nephew Muršili III, who fled to Egypt; when Ḫattušili demanded his extradition, Ramesses denied any knowledge of his whereabouts, and the two empires came close to war. The two versions of the treaty disagree on one point: the Hittite text says the Egyptians came suing for peace, the Egyptian text the reverse.

His monuments carried his claims. He used art as propaganda for victories over foreigners, had the alleged rout of the Hittites at Kadesh repeated on temple walls, remodelled or usurped existing works, and displayed his cartouches even on buildings he did not construct. For Libya there are no detailed accounts of large campaigns, only generalised records of conquering and crushing, which may or may not refer to specific events.
sections.last:
In the 30th year of his reign Ramesses celebrated, by tradition, the Sed festival, a jubilee held to honour and rejuvenate the pharaoh's strength. Such festivals were traditionally repeated every three years; Ramesses, who sometimes held them after two, celebrated thirteen or fourteen, more than any other pharaoh. As of Year 28 he favoured the god Amun above all other divinities, as two ostraca from Deir el-Medina show. With the northern border quiet after the treaty, his rule remained strong until his death.

By then, aged about 90, he suffered from severe dental problems, arthritis, hardening of the arteries and heart disease, and scans of the mummy indicate that he may have walked with a pronounced stoop. The cause of death is unknown; one possibility is the rupture of an abscess in his jaw, though researchers add that this cannot be determined with certainty. The last dated record of the reign is Year 67, first month of Akhet, day 18. A necropolis journal from Deir el-Medina records the "Sailing" of the king, a euphemism for his death, on the sixth day of the second month, which has been equated with 13 August 1213 BCE, after 66 years and 74 days on the throne; Jürgen von Beckerath placed the death in late July or early August, and Peter J. Brand in mid-July. Brand holds that he died in the north of Egypt, most likely at Pi-Ramesses.

He was buried in tomb KV7 in the Valley of the Kings and was succeeded by his son Merneptah. Some of his estimated 52 sons, among them his first-born, Amun-her-khepeshef, are believed to have been buried in tomb KV5.
sections.legacy:
Later pharaohs called him the "Great God" and prayed to enjoy his longevity; Ramesses IV asked the gods at Abydos to double for him the lifespan and reign of Ramesses II. He is often regarded as the greatest and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, though the dynasty waned after his death. Greek sources called him Ozymandias, from the first part of his regnal name, Usermaatre Setepenre; Diodorus Siculus quotes an inscription, "King of Kings am I, Osymandias", which Percy Bysshe Shelley paraphrased in his poem "Ozymandias".

Because of looting, priests moved his body from KV7 to the tomb of queen Ahmose Inhapy and then to that of the high priest Pinedjem II; it was found in 1881 in tomb TT320. In 1976 the mummy was taken to Paris for treatment and returned to Egypt in May 1977. A forensic study there by Pierre-Fernand Ceccaldi concluded from its red hair and cranial features that the king was of a "Berber type"; Cheikh Anta Diop disputed the result, arguing that hair morphology cannot determine the ethnicity of a mummy. In April 2021 the mummy was moved to the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo in the Pharaohs' Golden Parade. Abu Simbel, its facade almost covered by sand, was found in 1813 by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt.

Films and popular media often cast him as the pharaoh of the Exodus. Scholars generally do not recognise the biblical account as a historical event, and Egyptologists dispute the identification; the historian Lester L. Grabbe writes that an Egypt devastated by plagues is not compatible with everything known about this ruler.

summary: Ramesses II ruled Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BCE, the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh. He fought the Hittites at Kadesh, made peace with them in his twenty-first year, and built Pi-Ramesses, the Ramesseum and Abu Simbel. Later kings prayed for his longevity, and the Greeks remembered him as Ozymandias.
references: Peter J. Brand, Ramesses II, Egypt's Ultimate Pharaoh (Lockwood Press, 2023)
T. G. H. James, Ramesses II (Friedman/Fairfax, 2002)
Aidan Dodson, The Complete Royal Families of Ancient Egypt (Thames & Hudson, 2004)
Michael Gerald Hasel, Domination and Resistance: Egyptian Military Activity in the Southern Levant, 1300–1185 BC (Brill, 1998)
notes: Era written BCE (the article writes BC), as in the guide's examples; year numbers unchanged.

Birth: the article gives only 'c. 1303 BC' and no birthplace; 'far north-eastern nome' is Yurco's view as reported under Mummy. The article does not name his mother (Tuya appears only in a novel's cast list), so she is left out.

Death date: the article gives 13 August 1213 BC (Demarée/Peden reckoning), von Beckerath 'late July or early August', and Brand 'mid-July, ca. 1213 BCE'; all three are given. endCirca left false since all agree on 1213.

Age: lead says accession at 25 (1279) and birth c. 1303 (which would make him about 24); Nubian campaign 'when about 22' with two sons; prince regent 'at about fourteen'. Given as the article has them.

Chronology of the Syrian campaigns is muddled in the article: seventh-year campaign dated April/May 1272 BC, eighth and ninth years' Dapur campaign, yet 'by November 1272 BC back in Egypt'; tenth year 1269 BC. I dated only the 1272 campaign in the events and gave the rest by regnal year.

The 1274 event and the Kadesh result: lead says 'generally considered a stalemate'; the body says the Hittites were 'the ultimate victors as far as the overall campaign was concerned'. Both are given in 'opponents'.

Left out: Ali Gomaa's 2020 claim of suffocation and Hawass's reply; the 2006 hair theft; the recent finds (2018 booth, 2019 bust, 2023 sarcophagus fragment, 2024 sword); the Ramesseum and Nefertari tomb descriptions; the fiction list.

Wanted but not in the article: his mother's name; number of wives and daughters; the Hittite marriage; details of the reign's administration; any internal opposition; the names of the crown princes who died before him and why Merneptah (which son in order) succeeded.
